newsitem.title: ITALY: Castro plans to join food summit, Gaddafi may come.
newsitem.headline: Castro plans to join food summit, Gaddafi may come.

text.p: Cuban leader Fidel Castro plans to attend the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation's World Food Summit in Rome next week and the FAO's chief said on Friday he could not rule out participation by Libya's Muammar Gaddafi.
"We have information that...Castro intends to come and attend the summit," FAO director general Jacques Diouf said after meeting Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi.

Asked about an Italian newspaper report that Gaddafi was also expected, Diouf told a news conference: "So far I have not yet a list of the members of the Libyan delegation so I can neither confirm nor deny this information."
An official at the Libyan embassy could not say whether Gaddafi, whose country is under limited U.N. sanctions and stands accused by Washington of backing terrorism, would be coming to Rome.

While Diouf's remarks fell short of outright confirmation that Castro would make the trip, diplomatic sources in Rome have said that the veteran Communist leader is scheduled to address the summit on November 15.
The Rome gathering, from November 13 to 17, will be the first time heads of state and government have come together to tackle the challenge of how to feed the world.
"It aims at raising awareness, to ensure that the leaders of countries do not look short term, that they don't wait until we have a crisis to do crisis management," Diouf said.
However, the leaders of the two most powerful nations -- the United States and Russia -- will be absent and many heads of state from the developed world are also staying away.

French President Jacques Chirac, a patron of the summit, intended to come but has other commitments and Prime Minister Alain Juppe is to attend in his place. Britain and Germany are sending only ministers.

"This is a summit of heads of state and government," Diouf declared in defence of FAO. He had been asked whether the gathering was not ill-timed, coming so soon after the U.S. elections and at a time when the world was "summitted-out".
"So far we have around 100 heads of state and government expected and it will be the first time in history that so many will meet in one place to talk about food security."
The U.N. agency and host nation Italy have not released names of those attending for security reasons.
But high-profile heads of state who have confirmed their attendance include Indonesia's President Suharto and Kenya's President Daniel Arap Moi.

Castro's presence could provide an opportunity for an historic meeting with Pope John Paul which could in turn lead to a visit by the Pontiff to the communist-ruled island, the only Spanish-speaking country in Latin America he has not visited.
Vatican Foreign Minister Jean-Louis Tauran visited Cuba last month and told reporters at the time that the Vatican had agreed to make arrangements for a Papal visit.

Though Castro's engagements are routinely unannounced, diplomatic sources say a hotel has been booked for the Cuban leader in Rome for November 12 to 18 and meetings tentatively scheduled with Prodi and Italian President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro.
FAO sources have reported that Castro could be offered a starring role at the food summit, a move sure to upset certain countries opposed to his Communist rule over Cuba.
Diouf said nothing had been decided. "The posts will be decided by the summit itself and I cannot say exactly what will happen to that effect," he said.
